title: Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck

paper.title: Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck
paper.abstract:
Abstract Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful.
In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition.
Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case.
Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ) have become a major paradigm for high-quality image generation Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , text-to-image synthesis Rombach et al. (2022) and 3D generation ( Woo et al., 2024 ) . With the development of conditional diffusion models, the generation process can be effectively controlled by class labels Ho (2022) ; Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , textual descriptions Balaji et al. (2022) ; Ramesh et al. (2022) , or other forms of prior information. Among existing conditioning methods, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) Ho (2022) has become one of the most widely used mechanisms for conditional generation. Most existing CFG-based methods are applied with a fixed guidance strategy throughout inference, implicitly assuming that conditional information is equally important across all denoising stages. However, this assumption may be overly simplistic, as the relevance of conditional information is likely to evolve over time, which is a phenomenon that remains insufficiently understood. Although several recent methods have attempted to improve this design through dynamic guidance strategies, such as time-dependent reweighting Malarz et al. (2025) ; Poleski et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2026) ; Zheng et al. (2026b) , fixed interval activation Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) , or modified guidance dynamics Wang et al. (2026) ; Sadat et al. (2025) , these approaches still rely largely on heuristic schedules. In particular, it remains unclear how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves during generation, and hence when conditional guidance should be activated most effectively. Diffusion models generate samples by learning a reverse denoising process that progressively reconstructs the target data distribution. For conditional generation, the key question is how to inject conditioning information into this process effectively. Early approaches such as classifier guidance Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , as well as more recent TFG-style methods Ye et al. (2024) ; Shen et al. (2024) , use external classifiers to provide conditional gradients, but they often struggle to remain stable under heavy noise. By contrast, CFG Ho (2022) incorporates conditional information directly into training by jointly learning conditional and unconditional branches, making it more robust and practically appealing. Based on CFG, a series of variant methods replaces the unconditional output with alternative degraded references, such as the prediction of an under-trained conditional network Karras et al. (2024) or that of a conditional network with perturbed conditioning inputs Rajabi et al. (2025) . These approaches preserve the general guidance form of comparing a target conditional prediction against a weaker reference, while modifying how the reference branch is constructed. Taken together, these conditioning and guidance strategies highlight that the effectiveness of guidance depends not only on how conditional information is injected, but also on when it becomes most relevant to the denoising dynamics. This raises a more fundamental question: what are the benefits of properly scheduling the injection of conditional information, and how can this be understood from a theoretical perspective? To answer this, we investigate how conditional information propagates through a conditional diffusion model, and identify when it becomes most influential. We approach this problem through the lens of the information bottleneck, enabling a principled analysis of how conditioning signals are preserved and utilized across the denoising trajectory. In particular, we study the relationship between conditioning inputs and the score function, and establish a connection between mutual information and score-related statistics. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout inference; instead, it becomes significantly stronger only after a critical stage. Correspondingly, the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional predictions, together with changes in score norms, provides observable signatures of this phenomenon. These theoretical findings are consistent with empirical observations, suggesting that uniformly applying a fixed CFG strategy across the entire inference process is suboptimal. Building on these insights, we propose a dynamic CFG switching strategy for inference. Our key idea is to activate conditional guidance only when the generation process reaches the information bottleneck, so that the timing of condition injection is explicitly aligned with the theoretical analysis. The method is training-free and can be readily applied to a broad range of diffusion models and generation tasks, establishing a principled design criterion for CFG-based generation highlighting the differences and connections between various dynamic guidance strategies. In particular, it clarifies Interval Guidance Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) can be viewed through the same theoretical lens, offering insights into how we choose time to activate CFG. Extensive experiments on SiT Ma et al. (2024) ; Yu et al. (2025) , DiT Peebles and Xie (2022) , FLUX Labs et al. (2025) , and Stable Diffusion Rombach et al. (2022) ; Esser et al. (2024) show that our approach is both effective and broadly applicable. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • Information-Theoretic Perspective: We introduce a time-dependent information-bottleneck framework to investigate the role of conditional information throughout the diffusion trajectory. By connecting mutual information evolution with Fisher information, we derive a balance condition that characterizes an information-theoretically motivated transition region for CFG activation. • Principled Activation Criterion: Building on the theoretical analysis, we derive an observable guidance-gain statistic from the difference between conditional and unconditional score norms. We further develop a rescaled threshold criterion that improves numerical conditioning and provides an interpretable, model-dependent mechanism for identifying effective guidance activation regions. • Adaptive Guidance Strategy: We propose a training-free and plug-and-play dynamic CFG strategy that determines the activation time online through a threshold-crossing rule. Our framework accommodates both batch-level and single-sample inference, while recovering fixed-interval guidance in the large-batch concentration regime, thereby establishing a connection between adaptive and predetermined guidance schedules. • Extensive Empirical Validation: We conduct comprehensive experiments across diverse diffusion and flow-based architectures, including SiT, DiT, SD3, and FLUX. The results demonstrate improvements in generation quality under various evaluation settings, supported by multi-seed stability analyses, alternative activation criteria, and high-resolution single-sample inference experiments.

sections.heading: Diffusion Models and CFG.
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ) generate data by reversing a gradual noising process. In the continuous-time formulation, the forward diffusion process can be described by the following stochastic differential equation (SDE) Song et al. (2020b) : d ​ x t = f ⁡ ( x t , t ) ​ d ​ t + g ⁡ ( t ) ​ d ​ w t , \displaystyle\mathrm{d}x_{t}=f(x_{t},t)\,\mathrm{d}t+g(t)\,\mathrm{d}w_{t}, (1) where f ⁡ ( x t , t ) f(x_{t},t) is the drift coefficient, g ⁡ ( t ) g(t) is the diffusion coefficient, and w t w_{t} is a standard Wiener process. sections.heading: Mutual Information, Fisher Information, and Information Bottleneck (IB).
sections.text: To analyze the role of conditional information, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective. The mutual information Cover and Thomas (2005) between random variables X X and Y Y is defined as I ⁡ ( X , Y ) = 𝔼 p ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ [ log ⁡ p ⁡ ( x , y ) p ⁡ ( x ) ​ p ​ ( y ) ] , \displaystyle I(X;Y)=\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}\left[\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right], (4) which measures their statistical dependence. We also consider Fisher information, J ⁡ ( X ) = 𝔼 p ⁡ ( x ) ​ [ ‖ ∇ x ​ log ​ p ​ ( x ) ‖ 2 ] , J ⁡ ( X | Y ) = 𝔼 p ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ [ ‖ ∇ x ​ log ​ p ​ ( x | y ) ‖ 2 ] \displaystyle J(X)=\mathbb{E}_{p(x)}\left[\left\|\nabla_{x}\log p(x)\right\|^{2}\right],\quad J(X|Y)=\mathbb{E}_{p(x,y)}\left[\left\|\nabla_{x}\log p(x|y)\right\|^{2}\right] (5) which is directly related to score functions. Analogous to the decomposition of mutual information, the Fisher mutual information between X X and Y Y can be defined as J ⁡ ( X , Y ) = J ⁡ ( X | Y ) − J ⁡ ( X ) , \displaystyle J(X;Y)=J(X|Y)-J(X), (6) which quantifies the amount of Fisher information about X X explained by conditioning on Y Y . At last we introduce information bottleneck principle Tishby et al. (2000) , which formulates representation learning as a trade-off between compression and relevance. Given random variables X X and C C , IB seeks an intermediate representation T T that minimizes ℒ IB = I ⁡ ( X , T ) − β ​ I ​ ( T , C ) , β > 0 , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{IB}}=I(X;T)-\beta I(T;C),\quad\beta>0, (7) where β \beta is a Lagrange multiplier controlling the balance between compression of the input X X and preservation of information relevant to the target variable C C . Beyond its original formulation, the IB principle has also been used to interpret the training dynamics of neural networks ( Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015 ) . In this view, a neural network induces a Markov chain Y → X → X ^ Y\to X\to\hat{X} , where X ^ \hat{X} denotes the network representation or output. The learning objective can then be cast as an information bottleneck problem of the form ℒ ⁡ [ p ⁡ ( x ^ | x ) ] = I ⁡ ( X , X ^ ) − β ​ I ​ ( X ^ , Y ) , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}\left[p(\hat{x}|x)\right]=I(X;\hat{X})-\beta I(\hat{X};Y), (8) which trades off the complexity of the representation X ^ \hat{X} against its predictive power with respect to the labels Y Y . In our setting, this perspective provides a useful lens for understanding when conditional information becomes most important during generation.

sections.heading: Limitation.
sections.text: Theorem 2 applies only to stochastic interpolation paths with an independent Gaussian endpoint. It does not directly cover deterministic couplings, such as n n -rectified flow Liu et al. (2022) for n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 , where X t X_{t} is a deterministic function of X 0 X_{0} and the standard continuous information bottleneck may degenerate. Nevertheless, equation 20 can still be used as a practical heuristic in such models, although without the same rigorous information-theoretic justification. As for how to estimate score on Rectified Flow, a detailed discussion is provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 3.3 Justification via Hyperparameter Rescale
sections.text: Figure 1 : Sensitivity of the solution t ∗ t^{*} to the hyperparameter in the original and simplified formulations. The original parameterization ( red Δ ​ t \Delta t ) exhibits a much flatter log ⁡ β \log\beta – t t relationship than the rescaled version ( blue Δ ​ t \Delta t ), indicating higher sensitivity to perturbations. Notably, for a fixed perturbation in log ⁡ β \log\beta , the resulting deviation in t t ( Δ ​ t \Delta t ) is significantly larger in the original formulation. Experiments are conducted on SiT-XL/2. Despite its conceptual appeal, directly solving equation 16 in practice is challenging. The expectations in equation 16 are estimated using finite mini-batches during sampling, and involve squared score magnitudes, which are known to exhibit high variance. As a result, the empirical estimates of the Fisher information terms can be noisy and biased, especially at early diffusion times where score norms vary rapidly. To mitigate this issue, we propose a parameter renormalization perspective to solve the problem. (24) Comparing this with equation 22 , we establish a direct mapping between the original hyperparameter β \beta and the simplified hyperparameter β ∗ \beta^{*} : β ∗ = β 1 − η ⁡ ( t ) . \displaystyle\beta^{*}=\frac{\beta}{1-\eta(t)}. Figure 1 shows the relationship between log ⁡ β \log\beta and the corresponding solution t t for the original objective, as well as log ⁡ β ∗ \log\beta^{*} for the simplified objective. Solving the simplified problem with β ∗ \beta^{*} yields a solution t ∗ t^{*} that is asymptotically consistent with the original problem under β \beta . Since β \beta is already an empirical hyperparameter tuned for sample quality, absorbing the scaling factor ( 1 − η ⁡ ( t ) ) − 1 (1-\eta(t))^{-1} into the selection of β \beta incurs no loss of generality. This allows us to use the computationally accurate equation 22 as a proxy for the exact information bottleneck.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: Figure 2 : Overview of our adaptive CFG activation pipeline. Starting from noise, the diffusion model jointly evaluates conditional and unconditional scores at each reverse step, computes a guidance-gain statistic Δ ​ 𝒥 ​ ( t ) \Delta\mathcal{J}(t) , and activates classifier-free guidance only after the stopping criterion is met. The illustration uses a DiT/SiT-style diffusion backbone. Motivated by the theoretical and empirical analysis in Section 3 , we propose a practical procedure to determine when classifier-free guidance should be activated. Unlike fixed schedules, our method operates dynamically on a per-batch basis. Rather than explicitly solving the equilibrium condition in continuous time, we construct a stochastic process from mini-batch statistics of the learned score function. We then activate guidance at the first time this process crosses a prescribed threshold. An overview of the proposed sampling procedure is shown in Figure 2 . The figure illustrates how our method augments the standard reverse diffusion process with a batch-wise activation rule: at each step, the model jointly evaluates conditional and unconditional scores, estimates the guidance gain from their batch statistics, and turns on CFG only after the estimated gain exceeds the threshold implied by our information-bottleneck analysis. At each diffusion step t t , we perform a single forward pass by concatenating conditional and unconditional inputs within the same mini-batch, yielding score estimates s θ ​ ( x t , t , c ) s_{\theta}(x_{t},t,c) and s θ ​ ( x t , t , ∅ ) s_{\theta}(x_{t},t,\varnothing) . sections.heading: Relationship to Interval Guidance Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) .
sections.text: Our framework recovers Interval Guidance in the large-batch regime. As the batch size grows to ∞ \infty , the mini-batch score statistics in our thresholding rule concentrate, causing the random activation time τ activate \tau_{\mathrm{activate}} to approach a deterministic boundary common to all samples. This fixed boundary can be identified with the activation endpoint t h t_{h} used in Interval Guidance. Compared with Interval Guidance, however, our method does not require manually prescribing this boundary in finite-batch settings; instead, it infers the activation time adaptively from mini-batch score statistics, and the resulting rule is grounded in our information-bottleneck analysis. Furthermore, we explore the statistics properties of τ activate \tau_{\mathrm{activate}} in Appendix E .

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets and Models. We evaluate our method on class-conditional image generation and text-to-image synthesis. We conduct experiments on ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) and MS-COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . All models are based on advanced diffusion formula, including Flow Matching Lipman et al. (2022) (SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) ), DDPM Ho et al. (2020) (DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2022 ) ) and Rectified Flow Liu et al. (2022) (Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , FLUX ( Labs et al., 2025 ) ), using official pre-trained weights. Evaluation Metrics and Implementation Details. We use FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , sFID Ding et al. (2022) and IS ( Salimans et al., 2016 ) to assess both fidelity and conditional alignment. We use FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , Clip score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , HPSv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) and Aesthetic score Schuhmann (2023) for text-to-image tasks. All experiments are run on NVIDIA GPUs.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: In this work, we study Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) from Information Bottleneck perspective. We theoretically established that conditional information is not uniformly effective throughout the generation process but becomes critical only after a specific stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance. Based on this insight, we proposed a training-free, dynamic CFG strategy that adaptively activates guidance by monitoring score statistics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves sample quality and robustness across diverse architectures. There remain several promising directions for future research. Theoretically , as mentioned in Section 3 , while our Information Bottleneck analysis extends to stochastic flow models, extending the framework to fully characterize deterministic couplings would be an important next step toward a more complete understanding. Practically , while our method supports single-sample inference, batch averaging can improve the stability of the activation statistic. Developing more robust sample-specific criteria and extending the framework to heterogeneous conditioning scenarios remain promising directions for future research. Acknowledgment. sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: Conditional control in diffusion models is commonly achieved through classifier guidance (CG, [ 5 ] ) and classifier-free guidance (CFG, [ 12 ] ). CG introduces an external classifier to steer generation toward the target condition: ϵ ^ ( x t , t , y ) = ϵ θ ( x t , t , ∅ ) + ω Σ θ ( x t , t ) ∇ log p t ( y ∣ x t ) , \displaystyle\hat{\epsilon}(x_{t},t,y)=\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t,\varnothing)+\omega\,\Sigma_{\theta}(x_{t},t)\nabla\log p_{t}(y\mid x_{t}), (28) while CFG replaces the classifier with the difference between conditional and unconditional score estimates: ϵ ^ ​ ( x t , t , y ) = ω ⁡ [ ϵ θ ​ ( x t , t , y ) − ϵ θ ​ ( x t , t , ∅ ) ] + ϵ θ ​ ( x t , t , ∅ ) . \displaystyle\hat{\epsilon}(x_{t},t,y)=\omega\left[\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t,y)-\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t,\varnothing)\right]+\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{t},t,\varnothing). (29) In both cases, the guidance scale ω \omega controls the trade-off between fidelity and diversity. Owing to its simplicity and strong empirical performance, CFG has become the dominant guidance strategy in modern diffusion models [4]. However, most existing CFG-based methods apply a fixed guidance rule uniformly across all reverse diffusion steps, and recent studies have shown that this design is often suboptimal. A broad series of work therefore investigates dynamic or adaptive guidance strength . For example, [ 23 ] proposes a β \beta -adaptive strategy that enforces weak guidance in the early and late stages while strengthening it in the middle phase of denoising. [ 30 ] introduces Frequency-Decoupled Guidance (FDG), which applies different guidance strengths to low- and high-frequency components. [ 18 ] rescales CFG to alleviate over-exposure effects, while [ 25 ] proposes a geometry-aware normalization strategy to maintain stable guidance magnitude during late denoising. These methods suggest that guidance should vary with time or signal structure, and mainly focus on designing better weighting functions w ⁡ ( t ) w(t) or modified guidance parameterizations. To mitigate the computational cost of training distinct conditional and unconditional models, several approaches explore the idea of degrading the conditional network to mimic unconditionality. [ 13 ] achieves this by utilizing an under-trained state of the network, arguing that early-stopped weights contain less semantic bias and thus behave more unconditionally. In a complementary vein, [ 27 ] introduces stochasticity by adding noise to the conditioning tokens directly. By feeding corrupted inputs into the conditional network, the output becomes a degraded approximation of the true unconditional distribution, effectively replacing the need for a separate network. As for when to activate CFG, a representative example is Interval Guidance [ 14 ] , which shows that applying CFG over all denoising steps is suboptimal: guidance tends to harm diversity in the high-noise regime, has limited effect in the very low-noise regime, and is most beneficial only over an intermediate interval. Their method therefore restricts guidance to a fixed range of timesteps, improving both sample quality and distributional fidelity. While this line of work highlights the importance of when guidance is applied, existing methods still largely rely on hand-designed schedules or fixed activation intervals. Beyond schedule-based reweighting, another series of work revisits the guidance mechanism itself. CFG-Ctrl [ 42 ] formulates the denoising process as a dynamical system and interprets most existing CFG-based methods from a control-theoretic perspective, arguing that purely linear guidance may become unstable at large guidance scales and proposing a sliding-mode-control-based variant to improve robustness. In a different direction, Momentum Guidance [ 17 ] modifies the sampling dynamics by incorporating momentum into the CFG-adjusted flow update, providing a training-free and plug-and-play way to improve sampling robustness without retraining the model. Self-Guidance [ 16 ] instead derives an additional training-free guidance signal from temporal prediction discrepancies within the model itself, comparing predictions at the current and shifted timesteps and combining the resulting correction with CFG. On a more theoretical front, several recent works have begun to analyze the role of conditioning in diffusion models through the lens of information theory. [ 9 ] proposes an information-theoretic approach that maximizes the conditional mutual information to ensure the generation process retains maximum information about the measurements. Concurrently, [ 47 ] proposes the Dynamic Graph Information Bottleneck (DGIB) to learn robust and discriminative representations, defending against attacks on link prediction tasks. These studies align closely with our goal of adaptive activation, as both seek to identify the most informative moments for conditioning. Recent studies have explored information-theoretic principles to better understand and improve diffusion-based generative modeling. [ 34 , 48 ] generalize the connection between KL divergence ,Fisher divergence and Wasserstein distance to non-Gaussian isotropic noise perturbations, introducing a warm-started, variance-aware framework for tighter likelihood estimation and more stable diffusion training. More recently, Shen et al. [ 35 ] propose Rényi Diffusion Models, which formulate diffusion training through Rényi divergence and derive a generalized score-matching objective to explicitly control the trade-off between sample quality and distribution coverage. While these studies primarily investigate information-theoretic objectives for learning generative distributions, our work focuses on the role of conditional information during inference. Specifically, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and derive a Fisher-information balance condition to characterize an effective region for CFG activation. This leads to a training-free guidance strategy that dynamically determines when conditional guidance should be applied. Overall, these studies demonstrate that diffusion guidance can be improved by adjusting its strength, modifying its direction, or altering how guided updates are integrated over time. In contrast, our work focuses on adaptive guidance activation : rather than prescribing a fixed schedule or interval in advance, we study when conditional guidance should be activated based on the generation dynamics themselves. Notably, our formulation also provides a unified perspective on interval-based guidance, which can be interpreted as a special case under a limiting setting of our adaptive activation rule.

sections.heading: E.1 Properties of Stopping Time
sections.text: We collected a large-scale dataset of stopping times { τ i } i = 1 N \{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} for CFG activation on SiT-XL/2 ( log ⁡ β ∗ = 5.9 \log\beta^{*}=5.9 ). To characterize the stochastic nature of this stopping time, we fitted the empirical distribution of τ \tau against several candidate probability distributions, including Gamma, Log-Normal, Exponential, and Weibull distributions. Descriptive statistics of the collected dataset reveal a mean stopping time of τ ¯ ≈ 0.680 \bar{\tau}\approx 0.680 with a standard deviation of σ τ ≈ 0.050 \sigma_{\tau}\approx 0.050 . This indicates that while the stopping time exhibits a clear central tendency, it retains a moderate degree of variability across different sampling trajectories. The goodness of fit was evaluated using the log-likelihood metric. We find out that the Weibull distribution achieves the highest log-likelihood ( ℒ ≈ 713.24 \mathcal{L}\approx 713.24 ), significantly outperforming the Exponential ( ℒ ≈ − 268.89 \mathcal{L}\approx-268.89 ) and Gamma ( ℒ ≈ 675.64 \mathcal{L}\approx 675.64 ) baselines. This suggests that the optimal stopping time τ \tau in our diffusion sampling process follows a Weibull distribution with shape parameter k ≈ 16.78 k\approx 16.78 and scale parameter λ ≈ 0.70 \lambda\approx 0.70 . Figure 4 : Probability density function (PDF) of the stopping time τ \tau . The histogram represents the empirical distribution of sampled τ \tau values. The solid curve is the fitted Weibull PDF, and the dashed curve is the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) curve. The visual comparison presented in Figure 4 further corroborates the statistical findings. The histogram, which depicts the empirical frequency of τ \tau , aligns closely with both the Weibull PDF (solid line) and the KDE curve (dashed line). While the mean stopping time τ ¯ \bar{\tau} closely approximates the heuristic interval boundary t h = 0.7 t_{h}=0.7 used in prior art (e.g., Interval Guidance), the distribution reveals a crucial nuance. The survival function of the Weibull fit suggests that although the peak intensity occurs around 0.7 0.7 , there exists a “long tail" of activation events extending down to 0.4 0.4 . We evaluate a deterministic variant that uses the empirical mean stopping time ( t h = τ ¯ ≈ 0.68 t_{h}=\bar{\tau}\approx 0.68 ) against Interval Guidance and our proposed stochastic stopping method. While the mean-based threshold improves over the baseline, it remains inferior to the stochastic strategy, highlighting the importance of modeling the variability of stopping time. However, this deterministic variant still underperforms our proposed stochastic stopping strategy, which achieves the best overall FID. This observation highlights that while the average stopping time captures the central tendency of activation, it fails to account for the intrinsic variability revealed by the Weibull distribution. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models. † † footnotetext: ∗ \ast These authors contributed equally to this work. † † footnotetext: † \dagger Corresponding authors. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ) have become a major paradigm for high-quality image generation Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , text-to-image synthesis Rombach et al. (2022) and 3D generation ( Woo et al., 2024 ) . With the development of conditional diffusion models, the generation process can be effectively controlled by class labels Ho (2022) ; Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , textual descriptions Balaji et al. (2022) ; Ramesh et al. (2022) , or other forms of prior information. Among existing conditioning methods, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) Ho (2022) has become one of the most widely used mechanisms for conditional generation. Most existing CFG-based methods are applied with a fixed guidance strategy throughout inference, implicitly assuming that conditional information is equally important across all denoising stages. However, this assumption may be overly simplistic, as the relevance of conditional information is likely to evolve over time, which is a phenomenon that remains insufficiently understood. Although several recent methods have attempted to improve this design through dynamic guidance strategies, such as time-dependent reweighting Malarz et al. (2025) ; Poleski et al. (2025) ; Gao et al. (2026) ; Zheng et al. (2026b) , fixed interval activation Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) , or modified guidance dynamics Wang et al. (2026) ; Sadat et al. (2025) , these approaches still rely largely on heuristic schedules. In particular, it remains unclear how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves during generation, and hence when conditional guidance should be activated most effectively. Diffusion models generate samples by learning a reverse denoising process that progressively reconstructs the target data distribution. For conditional generation, the key question is how to inject conditioning information into this process effectively. Early approaches such as classifier guidance Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) , as well as more recent TFG-style methods Ye et al. (2024) ; Shen et al. (2024) , use external classifiers to provide conditional gradients, but they often struggle to remain stable under heavy noise. By contrast, CFG Ho (2022) incorporates conditional information directly into training by jointly learning conditional and unconditional branches, making it more robust and practically appealing. Based on CFG, a series of variant methods replaces the unconditional output with alternative degraded references, such as the prediction of an under-trained conditional network Karras et al. (2024) or that of a conditional network with perturbed conditioning inputs Rajabi et al. (2025) . These approaches preserve the general guidance form of comparing a target conditional prediction against a weaker reference, while modifying how the reference branch is constructed. Taken together, these conditioning and guidance strategies highlight that the effectiveness of guidance depends not only on how conditional information is injected, but also on when it becomes most relevant to the denoising dynamics. This raises a more fundamental question: what are the benefits of properly scheduling the injection of conditional information, and how can this be understood from a theoretical perspective? To answer this, we investigate how conditional information propagates through a conditional diffusion model, and identify when it becomes most influential. We approach this problem through the lens of the information bottleneck, enabling a principled analysis of how conditioning signals are preserved and utilized across the denoising trajectory. In particular, we study the relationship between conditioning inputs and the score function, and establish a connection between mutual information and score-related statistics. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout inference; instead, it becomes significantly stronger only after a critical stage. Correspondingly, the discrepancy between conditional and unconditional predictions, together with changes in score norms, provides observable signatures of this phenomenon. These theoretical findings are consistent with empirical observations, suggesting that uniformly applying a fixed CFG strategy across the entire inference process is suboptimal. Building on these insights, we propose a dynamic CFG switching strategy for inference. Our key idea is to activate conditional guidance only when the generation process reaches the information bottleneck, so that the timing of condition injection is explicitly aligned with the theoretical analysis. The method is training-free and can be readily applied to a broad range of diffusion models and generation tasks, establishing a principled design criterion for CFG-based generation highlighting the differences and connections between various dynamic guidance strategies. In particular, it clarifies Interval Guidance Kynkäänniemi et al. (2024) can be viewed through the same theoretical lens, offering insights into how we choose time to activate CFG. Extensive experiments on SiT Ma et al. (2024) ; Yu et al. (2025) , DiT Peebles and Xie (2022) , FLUX Labs et al. (2025) , and Stable Diffusion Rombach et al. (2022) ; Esser et al. (2024) show that our approach is both effective and broadly applicable. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • Information-Theoretic Perspective: We introduce a time-dependent information-bottleneck framework to investigate the role of conditional information throughout the diffusion trajectory. By connecting mutual information evolution with Fisher information, we derive a balance condition that characterizes an information-theoretically motivated transition region for CFG activation. • Principled Activation Criterion: Building on the theoretical analysis, we derive an observable guidance-gain statistic from the difference between conditional and unconditional score norms. We further develop a rescaled threshold criterion that improves numerical conditioning and provides an interpretable, model-dependent mechanism for identifying effective guidance activation regions. • Adaptive Guidance Strategy: We propose a training-free and plug-and-play dynamic CFG strategy that determines the activation time online through a threshold-crossing rule. Our framework accommodates both batch-level and single-sample inference, while recovering fixed-interval guidance in the large-batch concentration regime, thereby establishing a connection between adaptive and predetermined guidance schedules. • Extensive Empirical Validation: We conduct comprehensive experiments across diverse diffusion and flow-based architectures, including SiT, DiT, SD3, and FLUX. The results demonstrate improvements in generation quality under various evaluation settings, supported by multi-seed stability analyses, alternative activation criteria, and high-resolution single-sample inference experiments. 2 Background Diffusion Models and CFG.
